passages.passage_text: Upright posture depends on the integration of vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive input. A researcher measured postural sway in 12 healthy adults and in 12 adults with bilateral vestibular hypofunction, a reduced function of the inner-ear balance organs. Each participant stood barefoot on a force platform for 30 s under four conditions: eyes open on a firm surface (EO-Firm), eyes closed on a firm surface (EC-Firm), eyes open on a compliant foam pad (EO-Foam), and eyes closed on foam (EC-Foam). The foam pad distorts the signals that arise from the ankles and soles of the feet. Sway was quantified as the total path length, in centimeters, traveled by the center of pressure. A trial was stopped early if the participant stepped off the platform or grabbed a support rail. Mean sway path lengths are shown in Table 1. In the EC-Foam condition, 5 of the 12 participants with vestibular hypofunction had to end the trial early, whereas none of the healthy participants did.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Mean sway path length (cm)

| Condition | Healthy (n = 12) | Vestibular hypofunction (n = 12) |
|---|---|---|
| EO-Firm | 38 | 44 |
| EC-Firm | 52 | 78 |
| EO-Foam | 61 | 83 |
| EC-Foam | 97 | 241 |

questions.stem: Which condition requires postural control to depend most heavily on vestibular input?

options.A: EO-Firm, because vision and ankle signals both remain fully available to guide balance
options.B: EC-Firm, because removing vision leaves ankle and foot signals fully intact and reliable
options.C: EO-Foam, because vision remains available to compensate for the degraded ankle signals
options.D: EC-Foam, because vision is absent and the foam makes ankle and foot signals unreliable

questions.explanation: Correct: D) With eyes closed and a distorted somatosensory surface, the vestibular system is the only remaining reliable source of balance information. Why the others are wrong: A) All three systems are available here, so no one system is forced to dominate. B) Proprioceptive and tactile input from the firm surface can still stabilize posture, so the vestibular system is not the main cue. C) Vision is available to substitute for degraded ankle input, so vestibular reliance is reduced.
questions.trap: Choosing eyes-closed firm surface because it is the usual Romberg test, forgetting the foam also degrades proprioception.

questions.stem: In the EC-Foam condition, the mean sway path of the vestibular hypofunction group was approximately how many times that of the healthy group?
questions.explanation: Correct: A) 241 / 97 is approximately 2.5. Why the others are wrong: B) 1.5 would correspond to a path of about 145 cm. C) 2.0 would correspond to a path of about 194 cm. D) 3.5 would correspond to a path of about 340 cm.
questions.trap: Dividing 97 by 241 or subtracting values (144) instead of forming the ratio the stem asks for.

questions.stem: A participant tilts the head forward while standing still. Which structures primarily detect this change in head position relative to gravity?

options.A: The semicircular canals, in which hair cells are bent by endolymph moving during rotation of the head
options.B: The otolith organs, in which hair cells are covered by a gelatinous layer weighted with calcium carbonate crystals
options.C: The cochlea, in which hair cells are displaced by traveling waves along the basilar membrane after sound
options.D: The muscle spindles of the neck, in which sensory endings respond to a change in the tension of the tendons

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The utricle and saccule contain otoliths whose weight shifts with linear acceleration and static head tilt, bending hair cells. Why the others are wrong: A) The canals mainly report angular (rotational) acceleration, not static tilt. C) The cochlea transduces sound, not head position. D) Muscle spindles report muscle length, and tendon tension is reported by Golgi tendon organs, not spindles.
questions.trap: Assigning all balance functions to the semicircular canals instead of splitting rotation (canals) from tilt (otoliths).

questions.stem: Moving from EO-Firm to EC-Firm increased sway by 34 cm in the vestibular hypofunction group and by 14 cm in the healthy group. These data best support which conclusion?

options.A: People with vestibular loss rely more on proprioception than healthy adults do, since their eyes-closed sway grew less
options.B: Healthy adults rely less on vision because their vestibular and proprioceptive cues are fully redundant
options.C: People with vestibular loss rely more on vision to maintain posture
options.D: Vision is unnecessary for balance in either group, since neither group fell from the firm platform

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Removing vision hurt the vestibular group more, which indicates that they were leaning on vision to compensate for the missing vestibular signal. Why the others are wrong: A) Their sway grew by more (34 cm vs 14 cm), not less, so the data do not indicate greater proprioceptive reliance. B) Healthy adults also swayed more with eyes closed (+14 cm), so they still use vision to some degree. D) Both groups swayed more with eyes closed, so vision contributes to balance in both.
questions.trap: Reading any sway change as evidence of the other sense without checking its direction.

questions.stem: The foam pad is meant to degrade the information carried by receptors that signal changes in muscle length around the ankle. Which receptors are these?

options.A: Muscle spindles
options.B: Golgi tendon organs
options.C: Pacinian corpuscles
options.D: Merkel cells

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Muscle spindles lie within muscles and report stretch (length) and its rate of change. Why the others are wrong: B) Golgi tendon organs signal tension in tendons rather than length. C) Pacinian corpuscles respond to vibration and deep, rapidly changing pressure. D) Merkel cells respond to sustained light touch and texture.
questions.trap: Mixing up muscle spindles (length) with Golgi tendon organs (tension), both being proprioceptors.

passages.passage_text: The critical period hypothesis proposes that there is a window early in life during which language exposure is needed for full grammatical mastery. Deaf children born to hearing parents often meet sign language at widely different ages, which makes them a natural test of this idea. Researchers recruited 80 deaf adults who had used American Sign Language (ASL) as their primary language for at least 30 years and grouped them by age of first ASL exposure, with 20 per group. Participants between 45 and 55 years old completed a timed grammaticality judgment task of 100 ASL sentences, half grammatical and half containing a morphological error. Chance performance is 50% correct. Participants first exposed after age 13 had had little accessible language input before then. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Separately, a signer with a left inferior frontal lesion produced slow, effortful signing of short, ungrammatical phrases but responded appropriately to signed questions.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Grammaticality judgment accuracy

| Age of first ASL exposure (years) | Mean % correct | SD |
|---|---|---|
| 0-3 | 92 | 4 |
| 4-8 | 81 | 6 |
| 9-13 | 66 | 8 |
| 14-18 | 54 | 7 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Accuracy by age of first ASL exposure
graph.x_label: Midpoint of age of first exposure (years)

questions.stem: Which statement is best supported by the results?

options.A: Accuracy declines progressively as age of first exposure increases, with no sharp cutoff
options.B: Accuracy is unaffected by exposure before age 9, then drops abruptly to chance among later signers
options.C: Accuracy remains above 90% only in signers whose first exposure to ASL came from a deaf parent
options.D: Accuracy depends on the number of years of signing experience, which differs across the four groups

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Means fall steadily from 92 to 81 to 66 to 54, a graded decline consistent with a sensitive period rather than a hard boundary. Why the others are wrong: B) Accuracy already falls from 92 to 81 between the first two groups, and the oldest group (54%) is slightly above, not at, chance. C) Parental hearing status was not measured or compared in the study. D) All participants had at least 30 years of ASL use, so experience was roughly equated and cannot explain the pattern.
questions.trap: Reading a sensitive period as an abrupt on/off cutoff rather than a gradual decline.

questions.stem: The accuracy of the 14-18 group exceeds chance by what fraction of the amount by which the 0-3 group exceeds chance?

options.A: About 10%
options.B: About 25%
options.C: About 44%
options.D: About 58%

questions.explanation: Correct: A) (54 - 50) / (92 - 50) = 4 / 42, about 0.095 or roughly 10%. Why the others are wrong: B) 25% would require the later group to score about 60%. C) 44% is 4 divided by 9, not by 42. D) 58% would require a later-group score of roughly 74%.
questions.trap: Comparing raw scores (54/92 is about 59%) instead of the amount above the 50% chance floor.

questions.stem: The signer with a left inferior frontal lesion most likely has damage to which region, and which deficit does this produce?

options.A: Wernicke's area, producing fluent but meaningless language output with impaired comprehension
options.B: The arcuate fasciculus, producing fluent language with a selective inability to repeat heard speech
options.C: Broca's area, producing nonfluent language output with relatively preserved comprehension
options.D: The angular gyrus, producing an inability to read and write alongside normal spontaneous speech

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus supports production and grammar; lesions produce halting, agrammatic output with good comprehension, and this holds for signed language too. Why the others are wrong: A) Wernicke's lesions lie in the posterior superior temporal lobe and impair comprehension, which this signer retains. B) Arcuate fasciculus damage (conduction aphasia) spares fluency and comprehension but impairs repetition; the described output is not fluent. D) Angular gyrus damage is linked to alexia/agraphia, which does not match the signing deficit.
questions.trap: Equating aphasia with Wernicke's because comprehension is mentioned, ignoring the effortful output.

questions.stem: Which feature of the design most limits the conclusion that age of exposure causes differences in grammatical ability?

options.A: Participants were tested between 45 and 55 years of age, so aging itself would erase differences among the groups
options.B: The grammaticality task used 100 sentences, a number too small to allow the group means to be compared
options.C: Participants could not be randomly assigned to an age of first exposure, so family and schooling factors may be confounded with it
options.D: Participants all used ASL, a visual language, so the findings could never apply to the learning of any language

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Age of first exposure is a naturally occurring variable; factors such as parental hearing status, quality of early schooling, or additional disabilities could vary with it. Why the others are wrong: A) The testing ages were similar across groups, so age at test would not differentially erase group differences. B) 100 items with 20 participants per group is adequate for the observed 38-point range. D) Generalization to spoken language is a question of external validity, and the study does not claim ASL results are meaningless for other languages.
questions.trap: Blaming sample size when the actual problem is lack of random assignment.

passages.passage_text: The amygdala has been implicated in the rapid evaluation of threat, whereas the hippocampus supports the formation of explicit memories. To compare their roles, researchers tested 10 adults with bilateral amygdala damage, 10 adults with bilateral hippocampal damage, and 10 healthy controls in a fear-conditioning procedure. Participants viewed colored squares on a screen. A blue square (CS+) was repeatedly followed by a loud, aversive tone, whereas a yellow square (CS-) was never followed by the tone. Skin conductance response (SCR), a measure of sweat gland activity, was recorded during each square. After the session, participants were taken to a separate room and asked which square had predicted the tone. Mean SCRs, in microsiemens (uS), and the number of participants who correctly named the CS+ are shown in Table 1. All participants had normal hearing, and all rated the tone as unpleasant. Each square was shown 20 times in random order, and the first two presentations of each square were excluded from the SCR averages to remove orienting responses.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Fear conditioning results

| Group | SCR to CS+ (uS) | SCR to CS- (uS) | Correctly named CS+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Controls | 0.82 | 0.11 | 10 of 10 |
| Amygdala damage | 0.14 | 0.10 | 9 of 10 |
| Hippocampal damage | 0.78 | 0.12 | 3 of 10 |

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The amygdala is needed for explicit recall of the pairing, whereas the hippocampus is needed for the conditioned physiological response
options.B: The amygdala is needed for the conditioned physiological response, whereas the hippocampus is needed for explicit recall of the pairing
options.C: Both structures are needed for the conditioned response, since each lesion group differs from controls on at least one measure
options.D: Neither structure is needed for fear learning, because every group showed a larger SCR to the aversive tone than to silence

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Amygdala patients had no differential SCR yet knew the contingency; hippocampal patients had a normal SCR yet could not report it: a double dissociation. Why the others are wrong: A) This reverses the pattern: amygdala patients recalled the pairing (9 of 10) while hippocampal patients did not (3 of 10). C) Each lesion group differed from controls on only one measure, which indicates separate roles rather than both being needed for each response. D) Responses to the tone itself were not reported, and the CS+ versus CS- comparison shows an impairment in the amygdala group.
questions.trap: Treating an impairment on any measure as proof that the structure is needed for fear learning in general.

questions.stem: The difference between SCR to CS+ and CS- in controls was about how many times the same difference in the amygdala group?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) Controls: 0.82 - 0.11 = 0.71; amygdala: 0.14 - 0.10 = 0.04; 0.71 / 0.04 is about 18. Why the others are wrong: A) A ratio of 4 would require an amygdala-group difference of about 0.18 uS. C) A ratio of 9 would require an amygdala-group difference of about 0.08 uS. D) A ratio of 35 would require an amygdala-group difference of about 0.02 uS.
questions.trap: Dividing CS+ values (0.82/0.14 is about 6) instead of using the CS+ minus CS- differences.

questions.stem: Skin conductance increases during the CS+ because of activation of which division of the nervous system?

options.A: Sympathetic
options.B: Parasympathetic
options.C: Somatic
options.D: Enteric

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic fibers (cholinergic), so arousal raises skin conductance. Why the others are wrong: B) The parasympathetic division promotes rest-and-digest functions and does not drive sweating. C) The somatic division controls skeletal muscle. D) The enteric division governs the gut.
questions.trap: Assuming sympathetic activation always involves norepinephrine receptors, and so dismissing sweat glands as sympathetic targets.

questions.stem: Compared with controls, individuals with bilateral amygdala damage would most likely show which impairment?

options.A: Inability to form new explicit memories of events they experienced
options.B: Loss of the ability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision
options.C: Reduced ability to recognize fear in other people's facial expressions
options.D: Failure to experience any emotion, including pleasure and sadness

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The amygdala contributes to processing threat-related social signals, so lesions impair recognition of fearful faces. Why the others are wrong: A) Explicit memory formation relies on the hippocampus, which is intact in this group. B) Face recognition failure (prosopagnosia) reflects fusiform and related damage. D) Amygdala lesions blunt fear responses selectively; they do not abolish all emotions.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing amygdala damage to a total loss of emotional experience.

passages.passage_text: Learned helplessness is a pattern of passivity that follows exposure to aversive events that cannot be controlled. In a laboratory study, 60 rats were assigned to three groups of 20. Group E (escapable) received 64 mild tail shocks that could be terminated by pressing a lever. Group Y (yoked) was paired with a Group E rat and received shocks of identical timing and duration, but lever presses had no effect. Group N received no shock but was restrained for the same period. Twenty-four hours later, every rat was placed in a shuttle box in which a floor shock could be escaped by crossing to the other compartment. Rats were given 5 blocks of 6 trials. Escape latency, in seconds, was recorded for each trial, and a trial counted as a failure if the rat did not cross within 30 s. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Experimenters scoring latencies did not know which pretreatment each rat had received, and all rats had been handled equally before the study.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Shuttle-box performance

| Group | Mean latency across blocks (s) | Rats failing on most trials |
|---|---|---|
| E (escapable) | 4.2 | 2 of 20 |
| Y (yoked) | 13.9 | 15 of 20 |
| N (no shock) | 4.2 | 2 of 20 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean escape latency by trial block

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of including Group Y?

options.A: To equate the amount and timing of shock across animals while varying only whether the shock was controllable
options.B: To determine whether the lever itself, as an object, becomes a conditioned stimulus for later shocks
options.C: To measure the effect of restraint on later behavior when no shock was ever delivered to the animals
options.D: To test whether yoked animals learn faster when the lever is paired with a tone rather than shock

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Because Group Y received exactly the shocks Group E did, a difference between them can be attributed to controllability. Why the others are wrong: B) The lever's conditioned properties were not tested. C) Restraint without shock is the purpose of Group N, not Group Y. D) No tone or learning-speed manipulation exists in the design.
questions.trap: Mistaking the yoked group for the no-shock control, which has a different job.

questions.stem: By Block 5, the mean latency of Group Y was approximately how many times that of Group E?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) 16.8 / 3.2 = 5.25, about 5. Why the others are wrong: A) 2 would imply about 6.4 s. B) 3 would imply about 9.6 s. D) 13 is the difference in the number of rats failing (15 - 2), not a latency ratio.
questions.trap: Using the 13-rat difference in failures instead of a latency ratio read from the graph.

questions.stem: The similar performance of Groups E and N supports which interpretation?

options.A: Helplessness arises from lack of control over shock, not from shock exposure alone
options.B: Helplessness arises from exposure to shock alone, regardless of whether the shock is controllable
options.C: Helplessness arises from restraint, because only restrained animals later failed to escape
options.D: Helplessness arises from practice, since animals with more trials always show longer latencies

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Group E got the same shocks as Group Y but escaped normally, and Group N matched it, so controllability is the critical variable. Why the others are wrong: B) Group E received shock and did not become helpless, which contradicts this. C) All three groups were restrained or placed in the apparatus, yet only Group Y failed. D) Groups E and N had decreasing latencies across blocks, so more trials did not lengthen latency.
questions.trap: Attributing the effect to the shock itself rather than to its uncontrollability.

questions.stem: In humans, an explanatory style most associated with depression after uncontrollable negative events attributes the cause to which kind of factor?

options.A: External, stable, and global
options.B: Internal, unstable, and specific
options.C: External, unstable, and specific
options.D: Internal, stable, and global

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The reformulated model predicts that attributing failures to oneself (internal), as lasting (stable), and as affecting many areas (global) produces helplessness and depression. Why the others are wrong: A) An external cause does not implicate the self, which lowers the risk. B) An unstable, specific cause limits expected impact to one situation. C) External, unstable, and specific attributions are the most protective style.
questions.trap: Selecting 'internal' alone without checking stability and globality.

questions.stem: In Group E, pressing the lever to end the shock is best described as which type of learning process?

options.A: Positive punishment, because the aversive shock is presented after the lever is pressed
options.B: Negative reinforcement, because removing an aversive stimulus increases the likelihood of the response
options.C: Positive reinforcement, because the animal gains a pleasant stimulus after the lever is pressed
options.D: Negative punishment, because a rewarding stimulus is withdrawn after the lever is pressed

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Terminating shock strengthens pressing: a response followed by removal of an aversive stimulus. Why the others are wrong: A) Punishment would reduce pressing, not increase it. C) No pleasant stimulus is added; an unpleasant one is removed. D) Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior, which does not fit.
questions.trap: Equating negative reinforcement with punishment because both involve something unpleasant.

passages.passage_text: Deindividuation is a state of reduced self-awareness and accountability that can occur when people feel anonymous within a group. A researcher tested whether anonymity increases aggression more in groups than in individuals. Participants were told the study examined the effects of noise on learning. In each session, either one participant (alone) or four participants (group) served as teachers who pressed a button to deliver an unpleasant burst of noise to a learner, a confederate, each time he erred on a word task. Teachers chose how long to hold the button. In the identifiable condition, teachers wore name tags in a brightly lit room and the experimenter recorded who pressed. In the anonymous condition, teachers wore identical hooded coats in a dim room and responses were pooled so individual presses were not recorded. Each of the four cells contained 32 participants. Mean duration per press, in seconds, is shown in Table 1.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Mean duration of noise press (s)

| Condition | Alone | Group of four |
|---|---|---|
| Identifiable | 1.8 | 2.3 |
| Anonymous | 2.1 | 4.0 |

questions.stem: Which process best explains why press durations were longest among anonymous group members?

options.A: Increased self-monitoring, which makes people comply more strongly with the group's expectations about aggression
options.B: Reduced self-awareness and accountability, which weakens the restraint that usually comes from personal norms
options.C: Cognitive dissonance, which makes people justify the noise bursts by raising their liking for the learner
options.D: Social facilitation, which improves performance on a well-learned task whenever others are watching the individual

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Anonymity within a group lowers private self-awareness and perceived accountability, so behavior is guided less by internal standards. Why the others are wrong: A) Deindividuation lowers, not raises, self-monitoring. C) Dissonance would predict attitude change after an act, not more aggression because of anonymity. D) Social facilitation depends on evaluation by others, which was removed in the anonymous condition.
questions.trap: Confusing deindividuation with social facilitation because both involve being in the presence of others.

questions.stem: Among participants in groups, by approximately what percent did anonymity increase mean press duration relative to the identifiable condition?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) (4.0 - 2.3) / 2.3 = 0.74, an increase of about 74%. Why the others are wrong: A) 43% results from dividing 1.7 by 4.0, the wrong base. C) 174% is the new value as a percentage of the old one, not the increase. D) 1.7% is the raw difference in seconds misread as a percentage.
questions.trap: Dividing the 1.7 s difference by the anonymous value (4.0) rather than by the baseline identifiable value.

questions.stem: Which pattern in Table 1 indicates that the effect of anonymity depends on group size?

options.A: Group sessions produced longer presses than alone sessions in both the identifiable and anonymous conditions
options.B: Anonymity raised press duration by 1.7 s in groups but by only 0.3 s for individuals alone
options.C: Anonymous participants pressed longer than identifiable participants regardless of whether they were in groups
options.D: Press durations in the alone sessions were shorter than those in the group sessions across all four cells

questions.explanation: Correct: B) A difference of differences (1.7 vs 0.3) is an interaction: anonymity matters mostly when people are in a group. Why the others are wrong: A) This is a main effect of group size; it would occur even without an interaction. C) Anonymous participants alone pressed only 0.3 s longer, a small difference that does not show a consistent effect of anonymity. D) This restates the group-size main effect and says nothing about whether anonymity's effect changes with group size.
questions.trap: Reading two main effects as an interaction.

questions.stem: Which added condition would best test whether diffusion of responsibility, rather than anonymity itself, explains the long presses in anonymous groups?

options.A: An alone condition in which participants wear hoods in a dim room and are told their presses will be recorded
options.B: A group condition in which the learner is replaced with a second confederate who performs poorly on the task
options.C: A group condition in which all members wear name tags in a brightly lit room and the learner makes no errors
options.D: A group condition in which each member's presses are recorded individually but members still wear hoods in a dim room

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Keeping anonymity of appearance but restoring individual accountability separates visual anonymity from shared responsibility. Why the others are wrong: A) This tests recording in the alone setting, so it cannot address group responsibility. B) Changing the confederate tests a different variable (provocation). C) With no errors there are no presses to measure, so no behavior can be compared.
questions.trap: Changing the learner instead of the accountability manipulation.

passages.passage_text: Social learning theory proposes that people acquire behaviors by observing models and the consequences those models receive. In an experiment modeled on classic work in this area, 80 children aged 5 to 6 were randomly assigned, 20 per group, to watch one of four 5-minute films. In three films, an adult model struck an inflatable doll with a mallet while shouting distinctive insults. In the rewarded film, the model was praised and given candy afterward. In the punished film, the model was scolded and spanked. In the no-consequences film, nothing followed the aggression. In the fourth film, the model played calmly with toys. Each child was then left alone for 10 min in a room containing the doll and mallet while observers behind one-way glass counted imitative aggressive acts (spontaneous performance). An experimenter then entered and offered a sticker for each act the child could reproduce from the film (incentive performance). Mean counts are shown in Table 1.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Mean imitative aggressive acts per child

| Film | Spontaneous | With incentive |
|---|---|---|
| Rewarded | 7.4 | 7.6 |
| Punished | 2.1 | 6.9 |
| No consequences | 5.8 | 6.7 |
| Calm play | 1.9 | 2.4 |

questions.stem: The change in the punished group after stickers were offered best illustrates which distinction?

options.A: Learning can occur only when the observer is directly reinforced, so performance mirrors earlier rewards
options.B: Learning depends on attention but not on retention, so performance is unaffected by later incentives
options.C: Learning can occur without being displayed, so performance depends on motivation as well as acquisition
options.D: Learning is complete once behavior is shown, so performance and acquisition are the same process

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Punished-model children had acquired the aggressive acts (6.9 under incentive) but suppressed them until motivated to show them. Why the others are wrong: A) Children were never directly reinforced for aggression, yet they learned it by observation. B) Retention was needed to reproduce the acts a week of testing later and the data show it was intact. D) If performance and acquisition were the same, incentives would not change the count.
questions.trap: Concluding that the children in the punished condition did not learn the acts because they did not perform them.

questions.stem: Children in the rewarded and punished films were influenced by consequences that they themselves never received. This is known as:

options.A: Stimulus generalization
options.B: Latent learning
options.C: Higher-order conditioning
options.D: Vicarious reinforcement and punishment

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Observing a model's outcome changes the observer's likelihood of imitating, even without personal reward or punishment. Why the others are wrong: A) Generalization is responding to stimuli similar to a conditioned stimulus. B) Latent learning is learning that is not expressed until a reward appears, without observing a model. C) Higher-order conditioning pairs a new stimulus with an already-conditioned stimulus.
questions.trap: Picking latent learning because the incentive revealed hidden learning, ignoring the stem's focus on observed consequences.

questions.stem: By what percent did the mean number of acts in the punished group increase when stickers were offered?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) (6.9 - 2.1) / 2.1 = 2.29, a 229% increase. Why the others are wrong: A) 30% results from dividing 2.1 by 6.9. C) 70% is not derived from either value. D) 329% is 6.9 as a percentage of 2.1, which includes the original amount.
questions.trap: Reporting 6.9/2.1 (329%) as the increase, forgetting to subtract the baseline.

questions.stem: Which is the most important limitation on generalizing these findings to real-world media violence?

options.A: Hitting an inflatable doll in a lab may not reflect harmful aggression toward real people in daily life
options.B: Random assignment to four films makes it impossible to know whether each group started with the same aggression
options.C: Counting acts with observers behind one-way glass is certain to alter the behavior of every child in the study
options.D: Using children aged 5 to 6 means the results could apply only to learning that occurs at those precise ages

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Aggression toward a toy designed to be hit has limited ecological validity as a measure of real violence. Why the others are wrong: B) Random assignment equates groups on average, which is its purpose. C) One-way glass is used precisely to minimize observer effects; the claim of certain alteration is unfounded. D) Age restricts generalization somewhat, but not to precisely those ages, and the doll issue is more critical.
questions.trap: Naming the sample age as the key problem when the measured behavior is the weaker link.

passages.passage_text: Stereotype threat is the concern about confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which can impair performance on tasks related to the stereotype. A researcher recruited 150 undergraduates who rated math as important to them and assigned them to five groups of 30. All completed a difficult 20-item math test in a quiet room. Women were assigned to one of three instructions. In the control condition, they were told the test was a problem-solving exercise. In the threat condition, they were told that the test had shown gender differences in the past. In the no-difference condition, they were told that the test had shown no gender differences. Men were assigned to the control or threat instructions. Participants also completed a brief measure of anxiety after the test. Mean scores (out of 20) are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Women in the threat condition also reported higher test anxiety than women in the control condition.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Mean score on the math test (SD)

| Group | Instruction | Mean score | SD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Women | Control | 11.6 | 3.1 |
| Women | Threat | 8.2 | 2.9 |
| Women | No difference | 11.9 | 3.0 |
| Men | Control | 11.8 | 3.2 |
| Men | Threat | 11.5 | 3.3 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean math score by instruction

questions.stem: The mean score of women in the threat condition was lower than that of women in the control condition by approximately what percent of the control mean?
questions.explanation: Correct: D) (11.6 - 8.2) / 11.6 = 3.4 / 11.6, about 29%. Why the others are wrong: A) 17% is 3.4 as a percentage of the 20-point maximum, not of the control mean. B) 34% would be 3.4 treated as a percentage. C) 41% is not produced by any of the given values.
questions.trap: Using the 20-point maximum (17%) as the base when the stem asks about the control mean.

questions.stem: Which interpretation of the women's results is best supported?

options.A: The lower performance reflects a fixed difference in ability, because women scored below men in the threat condition
options.B: The lower performance reflects less effort, because women who rated math as important quit the test early
options.C: The lower performance reflects the situation created by the instructions rather than a fixed difference in math ability
options.D: The lower performance reflects test anxiety only among men, because men scored lower in the threat condition

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The same women scored as well as men when told there were no gender differences (11.9), so ability itself cannot explain the threat-condition deficit. Why the others are wrong: A) Women with no-difference or control instructions matched men, so ability is not fixed at the lower level. B) No effort or quitting data are reported, and the participants all valued math. D) Men's scores were essentially unchanged by the threat instructions (11.8 vs 11.5).
questions.trap: Treating a group difference under one condition as evidence of an inherent ability difference.

questions.stem: Which statement about causal inference in this study is correct?

options.A: Effects of gender on scores are causal because the groups were of equal size, but effects of instructions are not
options.B: Effects of the instructions are not causal because the participants knew they were being tested on math skills
options.C: Effects of both gender and instructions are causal because the same 20-item test was given to every group
options.D: Effects of the instructions on women's scores are causal because assignment was random, but effects of gender are not because gender was not assigned

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Random assignment to instruction supports causal inference about instructions; gender is a quasi-independent variable. Why the others are wrong: A) Equal group size does not make gender causal; random assignment, which applies only to instructions, does. B) Awareness of the topic does not remove the benefit of randomization. C) Using one test for all groups controls the measure, but does not make gender assigned.
questions.trap: Believing equal cell sizes or a shared test confer causal inference for a non-manipulated variable.

questions.stem: Which pre-test intervention is most likely to reduce the effect of stereotype threat on performance?

options.A: Having test-takers write about how the test reveals their ability, which sharpens their focus on the test
options.B: Having test-takers read about past gender differences, which reminds them of the standard to meet
options.C: Having test-takers complete the test under time pressure, which prevents them from thinking about the stereotype
options.D: Having test-takers write about a personally important value, which broadens their self-concept

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Self-affirmation reduces the threat to self-integrity by reminding the person of other valued aspects of identity. Why the others are wrong: A) Emphasizing that the test diagnoses ability increases threat. B) Reminders of the stereotype increase threat. C) Time pressure adds stress and consumes working memory, which worsens the effect.
questions.trap: Assuming that more focus on the test helps performance when that focus is the source of the threat.

questions.stem: Women in the threat condition reported higher test anxiety. Which mechanism best links that anxiety to their lower scores?

options.A: Heightened arousal improves performance on complex tasks, but only up to the point at which scores plateau
options.B: Worry about confirming the stereotype uses working memory capacity that is needed to solve the problems
options.C: Anxiety causes participants to attribute their scores to luck, which makes them stop trying on the items
options.D: Anxiety increases the speed of processing, so women attempt more items and make more careless errors

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Stereotype threat is thought to impair performance by consuming working memory with evaluation-related worry. Why the others are wrong: A) Arousal at high levels impairs complex tasks (Yerkes-Dodson), and the stem describes a decline, not a plateau. C) Attribution to luck is not measured, and no data on effort or quitting appear in the study. D) No data on speed or attempted items are given, and anxiety generally disrupts rather than speeds careful reasoning.
questions.trap: Assuming arousal always aids performance.

passages.passage_text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and interpret information in ways that support existing beliefs. To study it in hiring, researchers recruited 90 experienced managers and randomly assigned 30 to each of three conditions. All read the same one-page resume for an analyst position. Only a cover note differed. In the positive condition, a note said that a trusted colleague considered the candidate outstanding. In the negative condition, a note said that a colleague had concerns about the candidate's reliability. In the neutral condition, no note was included. Each manager then selected five interview questions from a list of ten, of which five probed strengths and five probed weaknesses. A question was counted as expectation-consistent if it probed strengths in the positive condition or weaknesses in the negative condition; in the neutral condition, strength questions were counted as a reference. Managers then watched an identical scripted video interview and rated the candidate from 1 to 10. Results are shown in Table 1.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Question selection and ratings

| Condition | Managers choosing 3 or more expectation-consistent questions | Mean rating (1-10) |
|---|---|---|
| Positive note | 21 of 30 (70%) | 7.8 |
| No note | 15 of 30 (50%) | 6.4 |
| Negative note | 20 of 30 (67%) | 4.9 |

questions.stem: The ratings in Table 1, given that all managers saw an identical video, are best explained by which process?

options.A: Accurate updating on new evidence, because managers weighted the video more heavily than the note
options.B: Ambiguous answers being interpreted so as to fit the expectation created by the cover note
options.C: Attribution of the candidate's answers to the situation, because the interview was scripted for every manager
options.D: Reduced cognitive load in the neutral condition, because managers with no note could not make comparisons

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Identical evidence produced different judgments, indicating that the prior note biased the interpretation of the responses. Why the others are wrong: A) If managers had updated accurately, ratings would converge across conditions. C) Attribution of scripted answers to the situation would apply equally to every condition and would not produce different ratings. D) Cognitive load is not measured, and the neutral rating (6.4) lies between the other two.
questions.trap: Treating different ratings of the same video as differences in the candidate's performance.

questions.stem: How many more managers in the positive condition than in the no-note condition chose three or more expectation-consistent questions?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) 21 - 15 = 6. Why the others are wrong: A) 3 is the percentage-point gap divided by 10 or a miscount. B) 9 is not supported by the table. D) 21 is the total in the positive condition, not the difference.
questions.trap: Reading the positive-condition count (21) as the difference between conditions.

questions.stem: Suppose the managers had instead conducted live interviews and the candidate, faced with weakness-probing questions, performed poorly. This would most clearly illustrate:

options.A: The halo effect, because one strongly positive trait influences judgments about the candidate's other traits
options.B: The fundamental attribution error, because the interviewer blames the candidate's disposition for the poor outcome
options.C: The actor-observer bias, because the candidate attributes the performance to the situation rather than ability
options.D: A self-fulfilling prophecy, because the interviewer's expectation shaped the behavior that confirmed it

questions.explanation: Correct: D) When expectations elicit the very behavior expected, the prophecy fulfills itself (behavioral confirmation). Why the others are wrong: A) The halo effect concerns generalizing from a single positive trait, which is not what drove the poor performance. B) The fundamental attribution error might coexist, but the key feature here is the elicitation of the confirming behavior. C) Actor-observer bias concerns differences between explaining one's own and others' actions.
questions.trap: Selecting fundamental attribution error because the interviewer blames the candidate, overlooking the interviewer's causal role.

questions.stem: Which change to the hiring process would best reduce the influence of the cover note?

options.A: Allowing each interviewer to adapt questions to the candidate's strengths and weaknesses
options.B: Telling each interviewer to be careful to rate the candidate without forming an opinion
options.C: Asking every candidate the same pre-set questions and scoring answers with a fixed rubric
options.D: Giving interviewers a detailed summary of earlier colleagues' impressions to inform the interview

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Standardized questions and scoring limit selective information seeking and subjective interpretation. Why the others are wrong: A) Adaptive questioning gives the bias more room to operate. B) Simply instructing people to avoid bias has little effect on automatic processes. D) Colleague impressions are the very prior information that produces the bias.
questions.trap: Believing that awareness of bias alone is enough to prevent it.

passages.passage_text: Researchers contrasted two explanations of helping. The empathy-altruism hypothesis holds that empathic concern produces helping aimed at relieving another's distress. The negative-state relief model holds that people help to reduce their own distress. Eighty undergraduates were told they were observing, by closed-circuit video, a student named Elaine who received mild electric shocks during a task and was visibly distressed. Participants were asked whether they would take her place for the remaining trials. Before watching, empathy was manipulated: some participants were told that Elaine's values and interests were very similar to their own (high empathy), and others were told that they were very different (low empathy). Ease of escape was also manipulated: participants were told that they would watch only 2 trials (easy escape) or all 10 trials (difficult escape). Each of the four cells contained 20 participants. The number who volunteered to take Elaine's place is shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Participants volunteering to take Elaine's place (n = 20 per cell)

| Empathy | Easy escape | Difficult escape |
|---|---|---|
| High | 17 (85%) | 18 (90%) |
| Low | 4 (20%) | 13 (65%) |

graph.title: Figure 1. Percent volunteering by empathy and escape

questions.stem: Which result best supports the empathy-altruism hypothesis?

options.A: Low-empathy participants helped more when escape was difficult than when escape was easy
options.B: High-empathy participants helped at higher rates than low-empathy participants when escape was difficult
options.C: Participants in the difficult-escape condition helped more often than those in the easy-escape condition
options.D: High-empathy participants helped at similarly high rates whether escape was easy or difficult

questions.explanation: Correct: D) If help flows from concern for the victim, it should persist even when the helper could easily leave: 85% versus 90%. Why the others are wrong: A) Helping that depends on escape being difficult fits the negative-state relief model. B) A difference when escape is difficult shows an empathy effect but does not exclude self-interest, since escape was blocked. C) A main effect of difficulty is consistent with relief of personal distress and pools across empathy conditions.
questions.trap: Picking the option showing high empathy helps more than low empathy, which is true in both models when escape is hard.

questions.stem: Which result is best explained by the negative-state relief model?

options.A: Among high-empathy participants, helping stayed near 85% to 90% even when escape was easy
options.B: Among easy-escape participants, helping was much higher in the high-empathy group than in the low-empathy group
options.C: Among all participants, helping was at least 20% regardless of the empathy or escape condition
options.D: Among low-empathy participants, helping rose from 20% to 65% when escape became difficult

questions.explanation: Correct: D) When escape is blocked, observing the victim's suffering is aversive, so helping to end it (and one's own distress) becomes the best option. Why the others are wrong: A) Helping despite an easy exit is better explained by empathic concern. B) A gap between empathy groups in easy escape is predicted by the empathy-altruism hypothesis. C) A floor of 20% does not distinguish the models.
questions.trap: Treating any high rate of helping as evidence of self-interest.

questions.stem: Among the 40 low-empathy participants, what percent volunteered to take Elaine's place?
questions.explanation: Correct: D) (4 + 13) / 40 = 17 / 40 = 42.5%. Why the others are wrong: A) 20% is only the easy-escape cell. B) 52.5% would correspond to 21 helpers. C) 65% is only the difficult-escape cell.
questions.trap: Reporting a single cell instead of pooling the two low-empathy cells.

questions.stem: Table 1 shows that ease of escape affected helping mainly in one empathy condition. This pattern is best described as:

options.A: A main effect of empathy only, because high-empathy participants helped more in both escape conditions
options.B: A main effect of escape only, because difficult escape produced more helping in both empathy conditions
options.C: An interaction, because the effect of escape depended on the level of empathy
options.D: No effect of either variable, because the average for easy and difficult escape was the same in every row

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Escape mattered a lot for low-empathy participants (+45 points) and little for high-empathy ones (+5 points). Why the others are wrong: A) Empathy had a clear main effect, but the data also show a difference in the effect of escape across levels of empathy. B) The escape effect was large only at low empathy (+45) and small at high empathy (+5), so it is not uniform. D) Both variables had clear effects, and their rows do not average to the same value.
questions.trap: Naming a main effect when the size of one effect varies with the other variable.

passages.passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized trial of a sleep-hygiene smartphone app for chronic insomnia. Adults were randomly assigned 1:1 to the active app or to a sham app that looked similar and delivered general health tips. Assignment used a computer-generated sequence concealed from the staff who enrolled participants. Participants were not told which app was active. The outcome was the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI; 0 to 28, higher is worse) at 8 weeks, scored by an assessor unaware of group assignment. Values in Table 1 are for participants who completed 8 weeks. The difference in mean change between groups was -3.8 points (95% confidence interval, -5.1 to -2.5). Participants had met criteria for chronic insomnia for at least 3 months and did not use prescription sleep medication during the study. Figure 1 shows mean ISI over time among completers. Dropout was higher in the sham group, and several sham participants who dropped out reported that the app 'was not helping.'
passages.table_data:
Table 1. Trial results

| Arm | Randomized | Completed week 8 | Baseline ISI (SD) | Week 8 ISI (SD) | Mean change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Active app | 120 | 108 | 17.2 (3.1) | 11.0 (4.5) | -6.2 |
| Sham app | 120 | 96 | 17.0 (3.3) | 14.6 (4.8) | -2.4 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean ISI score over time

questions.stem: What is the primary advantage of using a sham app rather than a no-treatment control?

options.A: It guarantees that dropout will be identical across arms, since all participants receive an app of some kind
options.B: It eliminates sampling error in the outcome, since both groups use a device that matches in appearance
options.C: It lets participants remain unaware of their assignment, so expectation and attention effects are balanced across arms
options.D: It allows investigators to see participants' assignment sooner, since the sham app records usage patterns

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A sham controls for placebo effects and attention, and supports participant blinding. Why the others are wrong: A) Dropout was not equal; a sham does not guarantee equal retention. B) Sampling error arises from sample variability, not from the control type. D) Revealing assignment would defeat blinding and is not a benefit.
questions.trap: Believing that a placebo control guarantees equal retention or removes random error.

questions.stem: What percent of randomized participants completed week 8?
questions.explanation: Correct: D) (108 + 96) / 240 = 204 / 240 = 0.85. Why the others are wrong: A) 80% would be 192 completers. B) 90% would be 216 completers, and is the active arm's rate (108/120). C) 92% would be about 221 completers.
questions.trap: Reporting the active arm's completion rate (90%) instead of the overall rate.

questions.stem: What does the confidence interval of -5.1 to -2.5 for the difference in mean change indicate?

options.A: The interval includes 0, so no conclusion can be drawn about whether the active app outperforms the sham
options.B: The interval shows that 95% of individual participants improved by between 2.5 and 5.1 points
options.C: The interval excludes 0, so a difference of no effect is not compatible with the data at the 5% level
options.D: The interval shows a 95% probability that the next participant will improve by exactly 3.8 points

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A 95% CI that excludes the null value corresponds to p < 0.05 for the difference. Why the others are wrong: A) -5.1 to -2.5 does not include 0. B) A CI for a mean difference says nothing about the range of individual responses. D) A CI describes uncertainty in the mean difference, not a prediction for the next participant.
questions.trap: Interpreting a confidence interval as the range containing 95% of individuals.

questions.stem: Because dropout was higher in the sham group, which analysis would best preserve the benefits of randomization?

options.A: Analyzing only the 204 completers so that every analyzed participant received the full 8 weeks (per-protocol)
options.B: Excluding the sham participants who reported that the app was not helping from the analysis altogether
options.C: Analyzing all 240 participants in the groups to which they were assigned (intention-to-treat)
options.D: Replacing each missing sham participant with a new volunteer recruited after the trial had ended

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Intention-to-treat keeps groups comparable and limits attrition bias. Why the others are wrong: A) Completers-only analysis breaks randomization if dropouts differ systematically. B) Excluding participants on the basis of their opinion biases the result in favor of the active app. D) Replacement volunteers were not randomized, so they cannot restore comparability.
questions.trap: Choosing completers-only because it appears to match 'full treatment'.

questions.stem: Baseline ISI scores were 17.2 and 17.0 in the two arms. This similarity is most directly attributable to:

options.A: Allocation concealment, which guarantees that every participant characteristic is identical across arms
options.B: Random assignment, which tends to balance both known and unknown participant characteristics across arms
options.C: Assessor blinding, which prevents differences in baseline severity from arising across arms
options.D: Intention-to-treat analysis, which statistically adjusts the baseline scores so that they match

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Randomization makes systematic baseline imbalance unlikely, particularly with a large sample. Why the others are wrong: A) Allocation concealment prevents selection bias, and chance imbalance can still occur. C) Blinding of the assessor prevents measurement bias, not baseline imbalance. D) ITT concerns analysis populations and does not alter baseline scores.
questions.trap: Crediting blinding for baseline balance, when blinding addresses bias after assignment.

discrete.stem: A university requires a first-year seminar intended to teach study skills. Many students report that the seminar is where they made their closest friendships. According to the functionalist perspective, the friendships are best described as:

options.A: A latent function, because the friendships are an unintended consequence of the seminar's design
options.B: A manifest function, because the seminar was openly designed to produce friendships among students
options.C: A latent dysfunction, because they disrupt the seminar's stated purpose of teaching study skills
options.D: A manifest dysfunction, because they are a recognized and intended harm to the seminar's goals

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Latent functions are unintended, unannounced consequences of an institution; the friendships are an unplanned benefit. Why the others are wrong: B) Manifest functions are intended and recognized; the seminar's stated aim was study skills. C) Nothing suggests friendships harm the seminar, so they are not dysfunctions. D) Friendships were neither intended nor harmful.
discrete.trap: Treating any beneficial outcome as manifest, rather than checking whether it was intended.

discrete.stem: An assembly-line worker performs a single repetitive task, has no say in the design of the final product, and cannot keep or sell what she helps make. Which concept from Marxist theory best describes her situation?

options.A: Anomie, because the norms that once regulated her work have broken down and left her without guidance
options.B: False consciousness, because she wrongly believes that her interests are the same as those of the factory owners
options.C: Alienation from the product of her labor and from the production process
options.D: Cultural lag, because the material technology of her factory has advanced faster than the norms for using it

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Marx described alienation as the separation of workers from the products they create, the production process, other workers, and their own potential. Why the others are wrong: A) Anomie is Durkheim's concept of normlessness, not Marx's. B) False consciousness would require evidence that she misperceives her interests, which the stem does not give. D) Cultural lag (Ogburn) concerns the pace of material and nonmaterial culture, not worker control.
discrete.trap: Choosing anomie because it is the better-known term for disconnectedness at work.

discrete.stem: A sociologist using the conflict perspective would most likely argue that sorting students into college-preparatory and vocational tracks:

options.A: Efficiently matches students' abilities to the occupational roles that society needs filled most urgently
options.B: Reproduces existing class inequality by channeling advantaged students toward higher-status paths
options.C: Arises from teacher-student interactions in which labels gradually become self-fulfilling for each student
options.D: Reflects a rational, rule-based system that standardizes decisions through formal procedures and records

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Conflict theory emphasizes how institutions maintain the advantages of dominant groups, including through tracking. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the functionalist account, which stresses social efficiency. C) This is the symbolic interactionist account, which focuses on labeling in micro-level interaction. D) This describes Weber's bureaucratic rationalization, not a conflict critique of tracking.
discrete.trap: Attributing the functionalist 'efficient sorting' idea to conflict theory.

discrete.stem: A country has a crude birth rate of 22 per 1,000, a crude death rate of 7 per 1,000, and negligible net migration. Using the rule of 70, approximately how long will its population take to double?

options.A: About 47 years
options.B: About 15 years
options.C: About 32 years
options.D: About 100 years

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Natural increase = (22 - 7) / 1,000 = 1.5% per year, and 70 / 1.5 is about 47. Why the others are wrong: B) 15 comes from using the 15-per-1,000 difference directly as a percentage without converting. C) 32 comes from using only the birth rate (70 / 2.2). D) 100 comes from using only the death rate (70 / 0.7).
discrete.trap: Using the crude birth rate alone instead of the rate of natural increase.

discrete.stem: A country's total fertility rate has been at about the replacement level for 20 years, yet its population continues to grow. The most likely explanation is:

options.A: A rising crude death rate, which increases the net number of people added each year to the population
options.B: A falling life expectancy, which raises the number of births each woman has during her lifetime
options.C: Population momentum, because a large cohort now of childbearing age keeps annual births above annual deaths
options.D: A declining proportion of women in the population, which raises the number of births per woman

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Past high fertility created large young cohorts; as they reach reproductive age, births exceed deaths even at replacement fertility. Why the others are wrong: A) A rising death rate would slow growth, not increase it. B) Falling life expectancy would not raise births per woman and would reduce growth. D) A smaller share of women would reduce total births, and fertility rate is already fixed at replacement.
discrete.trap: Assuming replacement-level fertility produces an immediately stable population size.

discrete.stem: In a population of 1,000, 250 people are under 15, 650 are 15 to 64, and 100 are 65 or older. What is the age dependency ratio?

options.A: About 15 per 100 working-age people
options.B: About 54 per 100 working-age people
options.C: About 35 per 100 working-age people
options.D: About 38 per 100 working-age people

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) (250 + 100) / 650 = 0.54, or 54 dependents per 100 people aged 15 to 64. Why the others are wrong: A) 15 counts only older adults (100 / 650). C) 35 divides the 350 dependents by the whole population (1,000). D) 38 counts only children (250 / 650).
discrete.trap: Dividing dependents by the total population rather than the working-age population.

discrete.stem: Residents of a neighborhood belong to a community organization whose members come from many income levels and occupations. Through acquaintances there, one resident learns of a job opening outside her usual circle. This is best described as:

options.A: Bonding social capital, which strengthens ties among members of a similar and close-knit group
options.B: Cultural capital, which consists of knowledge and tastes that signal membership in a social class
options.C: Human capital, which consists of the skills and training that increase an individual's productivity
options.D: Bridging social capital, which connects people across different social groups and supplies new information

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Bridging ties link people across social divisions and supply access to novel information and resources. Why the others are wrong: A) Bonding capital is within-group solidarity and would not supply information from outside her circle. B) Cultural capital concerns class-linked tastes and credentials, not network connections. C) Human capital refers to skills, not to relationships.
discrete.trap: Treating any network benefit as bonding capital.

discrete.stem: A woman inherits a title of nobility and later earns a medical degree. How should these two statuses be classified?

options.A: Nobility is an ascribed status, and being a physician is an achieved status
options.B: Nobility is an achieved status, and being a physician is an ascribed status because of the degree
options.C: Both are ascribed statuses, because social position is fixed at birth in every stratified society
options.D: Both are achieved statuses, because each is recognized by society after the person has acted

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily; achieved statuses are earned through effort or choice. Why the others are wrong: B) This reverses the two definitions. C) Medical training is earned, so it cannot be ascribed. D) An inherited title is not earned through individual action.
discrete.trap: Assuming that all statuses recognized by society are earned.

discrete.stem: According to the Davis-Moore thesis, surgeons are paid much more than most other workers because:

options.A: Unequal rewards motivate talented people to fill important positions that require long and costly training
options.B: Dominant groups restrict entry to high-paying positions in order to preserve their own privileges
options.C: Occupational prestige is determined mainly by the cultural capital that children inherit from parents
options.D: Wage differences are residues of past discrimination, which gradually disappear as markets modernize

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Davis and Moore argued that stratification is functional: unequal rewards ensure that the most important roles are filled by the most capable. Why the others are wrong: B) This is a conflict-theory explanation. C) This is Bourdieu's reproduction argument, not Davis-Moore. D) This is a different (discrimination and market) argument that does not feature in the thesis.
discrete.trap: Choosing the conflict explanation because inequality seems to favor the privileged.

discrete.stem: A listener can just barely detect an increase of 2 g when holding a 50 g weight. If Weber's law holds, approximately what increase would be just noticeable when holding a 200 g weight?

options.A: 2 g
options.B: 4 g
options.D: 8 g

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Weber's fraction = 2 / 50 = 0.04; 0.04 x 200 = 8 g. Why the others are wrong: A) 2 g would imply the difference threshold is constant, which Weber's law rejects. B) 4 g would imply the threshold doubles when the weight quadruples. C) 16 g would imply a fraction of 0.08.
discrete.trap: Assuming that the just-noticeable difference stays constant regardless of baseline intensity.

discrete.stem: A child watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, narrow glass and says the tall glass now holds more water. In Piaget's theory, this response is best explained by:

options.A: Preoperational thinking, which centers on one dimension, such as height, and lacks conservation
options.B: Sensorimotor thinking, in which the child has not yet formed an understanding of object permanence
options.C: Concrete operational thinking, in which the child can reason only about hypothetical or abstract problems
options.D: Formal operational thinking, in which the child overgeneralizes abstract rules to concrete situations

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Preoperational children center on a single salient feature and fail to conserve quantity across changes in appearance. Why the others are wrong: B) Sensorimotor children are infants and toddlers, and conservation tasks are beyond them. C) Concrete operational children succeed at conservation; the limitation described applies to abstraction. D) Formal operational thinkers reason abstractly and conserve easily.
discrete.trap: Selecting concrete operational because the task uses physical objects.

discrete.stem: A student who prepared well performs best with moderate anxiety but performs poorly with very high anxiety. Which idea is most consistent with this pattern?

options.A: Performance is best at an intermediate level of arousal, as described by the Yerkes-Dodson law
options.B: Performance increases steadily as drive increases, as described by drive-reduction theory
options.C: Physiological arousal follows the conscious experience of emotion, as described by the Cannon-Bard theory
options.D: Physiological arousal and emotion are independent and unrelated, as described by the James-Lange theory

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Yerkes-Dodson describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, especially for complex tasks. Why the others are wrong: B) A steady increase in performance would not predict a decline at high anxiety. C) Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur simultaneously and in parallel. D) James-Lange says that emotion follows arousal, not that they are unrelated.
discrete.trap: Matching any arousal-related theory of emotion to a question about performance.

discrete.stem: Two siblings share the same genetic risk for major depression. One develops the disorder after a severe job loss, and the other, who has faced no major stressors, does not. Which model best explains this pattern?

options.A: The dopamine hypothesis, in which excessive dopamine activity in mesolimbic pathways produces the disorder
options.B: The diathesis-stress model, in which an inherited vulnerability produces the disorder only when a stressor is present
options.C: The gene-environment correlation model, in which genes lead people to choose the environments they experience
options.D: The social-cognitive model, in which the disorder arises entirely from imitating the behavior of observed models

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Diathesis-stress holds that a predisposition and an environmental trigger interact to produce a disorder. Why the others are wrong: A) The dopamine hypothesis is mainly applied to schizophrenia, and the stem points to stress. C) Gene-environment correlation involves genes shaping exposure, which is not described here. D) Imitation of models is not the basis of the described difference.
discrete.trap: Reaching for a neurotransmitter hypothesis rather than a stress-vulnerability interaction.

discrete.stem: A canvasser asks residents to sign a petition for a park cleanup and returns a week later to ask the same residents for a $20 donation. These residents donate more often than residents asked only for the donation. The technique at work is:

options.A: Door-in-the-face, in which refusing a large request increases compliance with a later, smaller one
options.B: Foot-in-the-door, in which agreeing to a small request increases compliance with a larger one
options.C: Low-ball, in which commitment persists after the costs of the original agreement are raised
options.D: That's-not-all, in which a bonus is added to an offer before the person has responded to it

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Compliance with a small initial request (the petition) increases the chance of agreeing to a larger request later. Why the others are wrong: A) Door-in-the-face starts with a large request that is refused. C) Low-ball involves raising the cost after commitment, which did not occur. D) That's-not-all improves an offer before the target responds, which was not done.
discrete.trap: Mixing up foot-in-the-door with door-in-the-face because both involve two requests.

discrete.stem: A drug truly lowers blood pressure, but a trial with 15 patients per arm yields p = 0.12 and the researchers conclude it has no effect. Which error likely occurred, and what would reduce its probability?

options.A: Type II error; increasing the sample size would increase the statistical power of the trial design
options.B: Type I error; lowering the significance threshold would reduce the chance of detecting false effects
options.C: Type I error; increasing the sample size would reduce the chance of rejecting a true null hypothesis
options.D: Type II error; lowering the significance threshold would increase the chance of detecting true effects

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error; larger samples raise power and lower its probability. Why the others are wrong: B) A Type I error is rejecting a true null, which did not happen here. C) Type I error is not the mistake here, because the researchers did not claim an effect. D) Lowering alpha makes rejection harder, which raises the Type II error rate.
discrete.trap: Labeling a missed true effect as a Type I error.
